text:
'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
Did gyre and gimble in the wabe:
All mimsy were the borogoves,
And the mome raths outgrabe.

"Beware the Jabberwock, my son!
The jaws that bite, the claws that catch!
Beware the Jubjub bird, and shun
The frumious Bandersnatch!"

He took his vorpal sword in hand;
Long time the manxome foe he sought—
So rested he by the Tumtum tree
And stood awhile in thought.

And, as in uffish thought he stood,
The Jabberwock, with eyes of flame,
Came whiffling through the tulgey wood,
And burbled as it came!

One, two! One, two! And through and through
The vorpal blade went snicker-snack!
He left it dead, and with its head
He went galumphing back.

"And hast thou slain the Jabberwock?
Come to my arms, my beamish boy!
O frabjous day! Callooh! Callay!"
He chortled in his joy.

'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
Did gyre and gimble in the wabe:
All mimsy were the borogoves,
And the mome raths outgrabe.

'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
Did gyre and gimble in the wabe;
All mimsy were the borogoves,
And the mome raths outgrabe.

Beware the Quogg, my son! The jaws
That bite, the claws that catch!
Beware the Frumious Burblesnap, and shun
The whiffling Thrumble's match.

He took his vorpal blade in hand;
Long time the manxome foe he sought—
So rested he by Tulgey land,
And stood in uffish thought.

And as in uffish thought he stood,
The Quogg, with eyes of flame,
Came whiffling through the fennish wood,
And burbled as it came!

Snicker-snack! He swung his blade!
The vorpal edge went snicker-snack!
One, two! One, two! And through and through
The manxome Quogg lay back.

"Hast thou the Quogg?" the father cried.
"Come to my arms, my beamish boy!
O frabjous day! Callooh! Callay!"
He chortled in his joy.

'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
Did gyre and gimble in the wabe;
All mimsy were the borogoves,
As homeward went the boy.

In the tulgey wood where shadows creep,
There dwelt a Crollop, old and grim;
With vellumous hide and eyes so deep,
It prowled on legs so slim.

The woodsman came with axe in hand,
To fell the ancient tree;
But lo! The Crollop made its stand,
And snorfled wild and free.

"Begone!" it cried with burbled sound,
"This wabe is mine, you see!
I've gimbled long in this hallowed ground—
You'll not take it from me!"

The woodsman swung; the Crollop leapt;
They grappled through the fern;
With snicker-snack the battle crept,
And neither found return.

At last, exhausted, both did fall
Upon the mome-worn ground;
They gazed upon each other's thrall,
And neither made a sound.

They rose as friends when brillig came,
And shared the woodland bread;
The Crollop taught him all its game—
The snorfling paths ahead.

Now still they walk the tulgey way,
The woodsman and his friend;
And all the borogoves do say
Their friendship has no end.

There once was a Gribble most sprack,
Who'd figlet down every old track;
With a snibbet and snout,
It would scrim all about,
And scatter the glimmerwing pack.

The hunters pursued through the wood,
With spears and with bows, as they should;
But the Gribble so sly
Would wibble and fly
Through paths where no mortal man could.

One night in the tulgey, dark place,
The Gribble was caught in a space—
A cavern of stone,
Where it could not atone,
And death seemed to seal up its case.

But hark! The old Thrumble came near,
That creature of legend and fear;
It plored through the dark
With a luminous spark,
And the Gribble sang out in good cheer.

The Thrumble it opened the wall,
And out came the Gribble so small;
They burbled a song
As they danced all night long,
And the hunters heard nothing at all.

When morning did break on the wabe,
Two friends had escaped the dark cave;
The Gribble and Thrumble
Would never more stumble—
Together they'd dance, sing, and slave.

A Manxome Beast came lurgid through
The fennish and borogove-strewn ground;
Its eyes had a slithy, crollop hue,
And it gimbled without any sound.

No creature had ever beheld
Such terror, such fury combined;
The forest grew quiet, compelled
By this monster's vorpal mind.

A young girl with courage most bright
Approached with a song on her lips;
The Manxome Beast paused at the sight,
And burbled with curious lips.

"Why do you come here to our wood?"
She asked with a voice clear and true.
"I've wandered so long," said the brute, "as I should,
Seeking just one soul like you."

The girl took its claw in her hand,
Though all of the village said "Nay!"
Together they'd walk through the land,
And the monster no longer did stray.

Now gentle the Manxome Beast roams,
Through tulgey and wabe and the fern;
The girl made the forest its homes—
A lesson the elders could learn.

The Snibbet came snorfling by night,
A creature of mischief and glee;
It stole all the stars with its might,
And hid them in each tulgey tree.

The village fell dark in despair,
As moonlight and starlight grew dim;
The folk cried out into the air,
For hope was becoming quite slim.

A Beamish lad set out to find
The Snibbet and beg for the light;
He journeyed through wood, unconfined,
Through brillig and borogove night.

At last, in a clearing so wide,
He found the wee Snibbet at play,
Arranging the stars with such pride,
In patterns of splendid display.

"Please give us our stars back," he plead,
"Our village grows weary and cold."
The Snibbet, with whiffling speed,
Returned them—the sight to behold!

The lad returned home with the glow,
And the Snibbet came too to remain;
Now starlight and moonlight do show
On the boy and the beast on the wane.

Through wabe and through tulgey wood deep,
Came Thrombles with glimmerwing wings;
They'd gimble and gyre in their sleep,
And sing the most frabjous of things.

They danced in the borogove bower,
Where slithy toves did outgrabe;
Each night at their luminous hour,
They'd whiffle through mome-laden wabe.

But one Thromble was different, sad,
Excluded from all of the rest;
It burbled a song that was bad,
And plored through each tree at behest.

The others saw pain in its eyes,
And welcomed it into their throng;
Together they'd dance toward the skies,
And whiffle a vellumous song.

Now never a creature so lone
Must wander the tulgey wood bare;
For friendship is more than just bone—
'Tis kindness and love that we share.

'Twas brillig when the borogoves
Did gimble through the ancient wabe;
All mimsy were the slithy toves—
A peaceful, mome-ridden and grave.

A traveler came with vorpal blade,
Through fennish and figlet-marked ground;
He sought every beast in the glade,
For gold was the one thing he'd found.

He hunted the Quogg and the Crollop,
The Gribble that snorfled at night;
He'd snicker-snack every one down,
And burbled with greed and with might.

But lo! The old Thrumble arose,
More ancient than trees in the wood;
It snibbet and glimmerwing shows,
And faced down the man where it stood.

"No more shall you plunder this place!
The creatures are mine to protect!"
The Thrumble, with vellumous grace,
Had turned all the hunter's respect.

He dropped down his blade with a sigh,
And wept for the creatures he'd slain;
The Thrumble did burble and cry,
And healed all the woodland's pain.

Now man and the Thrumble do roam,
Together they guard the dark wood;
The forest, at last, has a home—
And all things are living as good.

'Twas brillig, and the slithy quoggs
Did gyre and gimble in the wabe;
All mimsy were the borogoves,
And the mome raths outgrabe.

"Beware the Thrumble, my dear son!
The jaws that bite, the claws that catch!
Beware the Sprack bird, and shun
The frumious Gribble's match!"

He took his vorpal blade in hand;
Long time the manxome foe he sought—
So rested he by Wibble-strand,
With uffish thoughts deeply fraught.

And as in fennish mood he stood,
A Lurgid creature burst the mere!
With eyes of flame through tulgey wood,
It burbled forth without a fear!

Snicker-snack! His blade went keen!
The Thrumble fell with one great blow!
A frabjous victory, bright and clean—
He chortled as he turned to go.

"And hast thou slain the Thrumble dread?
Come to my arms, my beamish boy!
O frabjous day! Callooh! Callay!"
He burbled in his triumph's joy.

'Twas brillig when he sailed the mere,
Through waters dim and dark and wide;
The vellumous waves drawing near,
With Sniblets glimmering on each side.

Past Crollop marshes, wet and drear,
Where Quoggs and Gribbles plored about,
He rowed without a sign of fear,
Through waters full of thrumbled bout.

The glimmerwings did dance and spark,
Above the blunder-strewn lagoon;
He navigated through the dark,
Beneath the pale and wibble moon.

Then homeward came the daring lad,
With tales of quoggs and waters strange;
His heart was full, his spirit glad,
Of all the wonders of the range.

Upon the marsh where toves once rowed,
A slithy creature made its way;
Through boggy banks and water-eroded,
It gallumphed through the gribbled day.

With mimsy fins and sprack tail wide,
It swam through reeds of tulgey green;
No vorpal threat could be espied,
Just peaceful waters, calm and clean.

The Sniblet sang a burbling song,
As through the fennish swamp it glode;
And all the Borogoves along
Did chortle at the slithy road.

The Wibbles floated, one by one,
Each vellumous and bright with gleam;
They danced beneath the water's sun,
Like fragments of a golden dream.

When brillig fell on Crollop mere,
The Gribbles made their way to rest;
With scrim of moss they had no fear,
Within the wabe's embrace, so blessed.

And there upon the marshy shore,
The creatures sang in harmony;
Of waters deep forevermore,
And all the joy of liberty.

In waters deep where currents flow,
A manxome Beast of lurgid kind
Did plore the depths, both high and low,
With whiffling gills of twisted mind.

Through borogove-thick reeds it wound,
Past Thrumbles sleeping on the bed;
No vorpal thing could e'er be found
To strike the creature cold and dead.

The Snorfling birds flew overhead,
With figlet wings of silver-bright;
They soared where vellumous things fled,
Through tulgey waters, day and night.

This Beast with beamish eyes so keen
Did swim through galleries of stone;
The strangest creature e'er was seen
In waters deep and dark and lone.

It burbled out a frabjous cry,
That echoed through the marshy plain;
And all the creatures passingby
Would chortle at its sweet refrain.

When brillig came once more around,
The Beast rose up from waters cold;
No snicker-snack would e'er resound—
It had a heart of gleaming gold.

It galumphed through the shallows bright,
With uffish pride and sprack elan;
And vanished in the fading light,
A legend born from water's span.

Beyond the sea where waters swirl,
A slithy Quogg of ancient days
Did through the borogove-thick furl,
And mome raths marked its winding ways.

With gribble-fins and tulgey-scaled,
It rode the waves both wild and free;
Through foam where Crollops never failed,
It rowed across the vellum sea.

The Sniblets danced upon the tide,
With mimsy movements, soft and low;
While Wibbles pirouetted wide,
In patterns none could ever know.

A manxome storm came burbling down,
The sky grew dark with scrim and dread;
Our slithy hero wore a crown
Of figlet-light upon its head.

With vorpal courage, bold and true,
It plowed through waters fierce and tall;
The Thrumbles watched as onward flew
This sprack and beamish creature tall.

It chortled through the worst of gale,
Its frabjous spirit could not break;
No snicker-snack nor fell travail
Could make this uffish Quogg awake.

And when at last the storm did pass,
And brillig settled on the sea,
It rested in the waters glass,
A hero wild and bold and free.

Across the marsh where Gribbles dwell,
A Figlet bird of vellum-wing
Did through the tulgey waters sail,
And burbled out a mournful sing.

With mimsy plumage, soft and grey,
It soared above the borogove;
Through waters dim throughout the day,
It searched for its long-lost old love.

The Wibbles floating all around
Could see the sorrow in its eyes;
Upon the marshy, fennish ground,
It burst into a sad reprise.

A Snorfling creature, old and wise,
Did offer counsel true and deep;
"Beyond yon scrim of waters lies
Your darling, in the Crollops' keep."

With sprack determination set,
The Figlet bird flew swift and true;
Through tulgey reeds that glistened wet,
Where lurgid things and strange things grew.

It found its love upon a shore,
Surrounded by the vorpal light;
They chortled, danced, and sang once more,
All through the brillig, beamish night.

With uffish joy they galumphed free,
No manxome threat could e'er arise;
They soared across the golden sea,
Beneath the gleaming wibble skies.

Deep in a marsh of mome and bight,
Where waters thick with snorfling mud
Did flow with uffish, mitten light,
And strange things stirred within the flood.

A Thrumble ancient, lurgid, vast,
With vellumous and gribbled hide,
Had through the years and ages passed
In wabe most tulgey, dark and wide.

It plored the depths with burbled song,
While Sniblets danced above its head;
For centuries it swam along,
Through waters where the Borogoves fled.

A young and sprack and beamish Quogg
Did come unto that mystic place;
It swam through every fenning bog,
With wonder written on its face.

"What ancient creature art thou here?"
It asked the Thrumble, old and wise;
The great Beast answered without fear,
With vorpal gleam within its eyes.

"I am the guardian of this stream,
The keeper of the water-way;
I've guarded all since ages dream,
Through every gribbled, figlet day."

The Quogg and Thrumble then became
The truest friends the marsh had known;
Together they would play the game,
And chortle through the brillig zone.

When danger came with snicker-snack,
They stood as one, both brave and true;
No manxome foe could turn them back,
These water-friends of lurgid hue.

And thus they lived in frabjous peace,
Within the waters deep and wide;
Their chortled joys would never cease,
As through the borogoves they glide.

'Twas brillig when the moonlight fell,
And slithy toves did gyre and wail,
Through tulgey woods where shadows dwell,
The mome raths danced beyond the veil.

The wibbles crept on fennish ground,
With glimmerwings of silver pale,
Each sprack and quogg made not a sound,
As mimsy borogoves did sail.

Come hither, lad, beware the night,
Where gribbles lurk in scrimmed repose,
The frabjous creatures dance from sight,
And thrumbles bloom where cold wind blows.

My son did gyre through dreamy sleep,
With vorpal sword held firm and true,
The glimmerwings did vigil keep,
While lurgid shadows fell on dew.

He burbled onward, uffish still,
Through wabe that shimmered, strange and far,
His heart was light, his wandering will,
Led outward toward the sleeping star.

At last he came to morning's gleam,
The toves had faded with the night,
He snicker-snacked away the dream,
And found himself in golden light.

Then down he sat with joy complete,
His journey through the dark was done,
The frabjous night made rest so sweet,
Before the rise of waking sun.

In moonlit glades the figlets sleep,
With crollop wings so soft and wide,
The fennish creatures, dark and deep,
Rest snug before the eventide.

'Twas brillig when the dream took hold,
And slumbering things began to stir,
The wibbles wore their mantles cold,
While sprack-like whispers seemed to blur.

A manxome beast came whiffling near,
With burbling voice both strange and low,
The sleeping souls drew back in fear,
Yet onward still the creature'd go.

But when the morning light appeared,
The glimmerwings had lost their might,
All tulgey dreams were strange and weird,
And faded with the fleeing night.

The borogoves began to dream,
Of places warm and blazing bright,
Their plored minds began to gleam,
As darkness swallowed up the night.

Yet in the hush of slumber deep,
Where slithy toves and quoggs belong,
The mimsy creatures, safe asleep,
Still hum their own nocturnal song.

The raths came snorfling through the dew,
With vellumous and sprack intent,
They sought the path the shadows knew,
Through wabe where moonbeams gently went.

When dawn broke forth with rosy glow,
The figlets stirred and came alive,
The crollop creatures, fast below,
Had made it through the night to thrive.

But still they dreamed of starry skies,
Of thrumbles dancing in the air,
Of lurgid nights and phantom sighs,
When moonlight flooded everywhere.

'Twas brillig in the witching hour,
When gribbles rose from earth below,
With frabjous grace and shadowed power,
They swayed in patterns soft and slow.

The toves came gyring through the night,
Their slithy forms like liquid shade,
They burbled songs of pure delight,
In moonlit glades where dreams were made.

A snibbet crept along the stone,
With whiffling breath and uffish grace,
It walked the path, but not alone,
Through tulgey dark and manxome space.

My son did chortled at the sight,
Of creatures dancing through the dream,
His vorpal courage burned so bright,
Against the shadows' gentle stream.

He galumphed through the wabe so wild,
With beamish heart and fearless soul,
A snicker-snack laugh, like a child,
Made broken darkness somehow whole.

The glimmerwings did guide him on,
Through plored and fennish, strange terrain,
Until the dream at last had gone,
And morning broke the dark's domain.

When brillig fades to morning's call,
The slithy toves creep back to ground,
The mimsy borogoves all,
Return to where they can't be found.

The wibbles rest through daylit hours,
In scrimmed retreats both safe and deep,
While figlets in their secret bowers,
Resume their long, enchanted sleep.

Yet when the dusk returns once more,
And moonlight creeps across the land,
The gribbles wake as they did before,
With lurgid hearts and shadowed hand.

The sprack and quogg will rise and play,
The toves will gyre their ancient dance,
The thrumbles hum through break of day,
And draw the sleeping into trance.

So here's to dreams and moon-pale night,
To creatures strange and burbled call,
To glimmerwings' ethereal light,
That holds dominion over all.

When brilliant stars do fade away,
And darkness claims the waking mind,
The toves and borogoves will stay,
And dreams in midnight we will find.

'Twas brillig, and the slithy cook
Did chop the toves with vorpal blade,
While borogoves in every nook
Went mimsy through the kitchen shade.

"Beware!" cried out the frumious maid,
"The quogg doth gyre about the stove!
It gyred and gimbled, unafraid,
And burbled through the hearth above."

With snicker-snack the tulgey pots
Did clatter on the fennish floor,
The gribbles gnawed their tangled knots,
While wibbles whiffled at the door.

The beamish boy came galumphing near,
His sprack young hands so vellumous and bright,
He chortled loud for all to hear,
"The snarks have fled! The wabe's alight!"

But still the lurgid thrumbles spun,
And figlets danced upon the sill,
Till mimsy shadows blocked the sun,
And all the crollops went quite still.

Then frabjous light did break the gloom,
The manxome magic came undone,
And order settled through the room,
As brillig faded with the sun.

The toves crept back into their wabe,
The uffish cook did sigh with cheer,
No more would outgrabe fill the glade,
For now came mome and raths sincere.

And still today in that strange place,
Where brillig cooks do snibble fast,
The glimmerwing with beamish grace,
Recalls that kitchen's blunder-past.

'Twas afternoon in Muggleton Fair,
When slithy gardeners came to till,
With toves and quoggs beyond compare,
They planted dreams on blunder-hill.

The vorpal hoe did snicker-snack,
Against the wabe's resistant ground,
While borogoves came ambling back,
With mimsy flowers all around.

"Plant not the tulgey raths!" they cried,
The frumious vines began to spread,
They gyred and gimbled far and wide,
Through every bed of white and red.

But still the burbled thrumbles grew,
With gribbles twined in wibble-knots,
The sprack young gardeners never knew,
What figured in those fenland plots.

The beamish sun beat down so bright,
Yet figlets came to steal the day,
Till manxome shadows fell at night,
And all the snorfling blooms gave way.

Then frabjous morning broke once more,
The uffish gardeners did cheer,
For crollops lined the garden door,
And outgrabe echoed sharp and clear.

The mome had whispered through the night,
A charm to make the gardens true,
And by the glimmerwing's pale light,
The flowers grew both old and new.

So every spring in Muggleton Fair,
The gallimaufry comes to play,
Where slithy things and toves so rare,
Do gyre throughout the livelong day.

In cottage hearth where brillig burns,
Old Grandmother did stir her stew,
While slithy servants made their turns,
And borogoves came into view.

The toves brought forth the vorpal meat,
With gribbles gnawing at the bone,
While mimsy vapors rose up sweet,
From wabe-stone bricks around the home.

"Come quick!" she called to all her kin,
"The quogg hath brought the raths at last!
The tulgey broth begins to spin,
And frumious spells are coming fast!"

The figlets fluttered through the steam,
Like wibbles dancing in the air,
The crollops twitched and shimmer-gleamed,
While fenland herbs perfumed the prayer.

They burbled songs around the fire,
The thrumbles beating soft and slow,
Each glimmerwing did gyre higher,
With snicker-snack and beamish glow.

When suppertime had come at last,
The manxome feast lay on the board,
And uffish tales of futures past,
Were outgrabe'd by each feasting lord.

Then through the brillig-darkened night,
The mome and raths crept back to rest,
While snorfling dreams of warm delight,
Left every heart supremely blessed.

Upon the fence in Wimbledon,
Where slithy birds did perch and caw,
The toves began their morning run,
And nothing broke a single law.

The wabe stretched wide, both green and long,
With borogoves that mimsy pranced,
While vorpal songbirds sang their song,
And everything enchanted danced.

But quogg came hopping through the gate,
With gribbles clinging to its back,
It burst with frumious, fierce hate,
And bent the fence with loud snack-snack.

The gardener rose with uffish dread,
The tulgey night came rushing on,
While figlets danced around his head,
And burbled all the light till dawn.

He grasped his manxome fighting tool,
The thrumbles scattered far and wide,
The crollops dove into the pool,
Where lurgid wibbles yet reside.

With snicker-snack the battle raged,
The glimmerwing broke through the sky,
The beast that once his heart had caged,
Went galloping with beamish cry.

Then frabjous peace came back at last,
The outgrabe faded from the ground,
The mome and raths in shadows passed,
And brillig silence wrapped around.

The fence stood mended, scarred but strong,
Where slithy birds returned to stay,
And still they warble sprack their song,
Upon each soft and fenland day.

In Tollerton the baker dwelt,
Who kneaded dough with hands so white,
'Twas brillig when the heat he felt,
And slithy ovens glowed so bright.

The toves crept in to steal the bread,
The borogoves would watch and wait,
While vorpal shears hung overhead,
And quoggs stood guard outside the gate.

"Beware the frumious midnight rise!"
The wabe-keeper would always say,
"For gribbles lurk with wibble eyes,
And raths come out to hunt by day."

The baker paid them little mind,
He kneaded, rolled, and shaped his art,
But figlets he would always find,
Pressed thumbprints on each tulgey part.

The thrumbles beat their snicker-snack,
Against the crollops in the bin,
While burbled songs came floating back,
Through every gap and every spin.

Then one dawn broke with beamish light,
The manxome bread had disappeared!
The uffish baker wept outright,
When outgrabe came as long he'd feared.

But in the wabe, so mome and deep,
Where snorfling creatures ever dwell,
He found his bread in glimmering heap,
And frabjous stories all to tell.

The raths had taken every loaf,
To feed their fenland cottages,
The baker shed his skeptic's scoff,
And baked for all those passages.

And so the brillig ovens gleamed,
With slithy commerce running true,
Where toves and gardens ever dreamed,
Of vorpal bread and friendship new.

Three sisters dwelt in Ribbleton,
Where slithy servants came each week,
The toves would gather one by one,
And borogoves would climb the peak.

They mended cloaks with mimsy thread,
And tulgey patches, worn and old,
The frumious needles danced and spread,
While wabe-light fell both bright and cold.

"The quoggs have gnawed the hem!" cried one,
The gribbles scattered from the sill,
The vorpal shears went snicker-snack,
As wibbles danced upon the mill.

The figlets tangled in the yarn,
The crollops leaped from cloth to cloth,
The thrumbles beat their warning warn,
While burbled clouds consumed them both.

The manxome seamstress worked on still,
Her glimmerwing fingers flew so fast,
She stitched with beamish, uffish skill,
Till outgrabe could not hold them fast.

With snorfling ghosts and mome delight,
The cloaks transformed to something strange,
They glowed with frabjous, lurgid light,
As if the world might wholly change.

Then brillig faded with the dew,
The slithy magic lost its hold,
And three sisters saw what they'd sewn through:
A tapestry of stories told.

The raths crept back beyond the hedge,
Where fenland mist rolls thick and deep,
The toves curled up upon the edge,
And all the world began to sleep.

In Fenshop Lane there lived a dame,
Who kept a root and herb garden strange,
The slithy vines all bore her name,
And toves moved through her wabe-range.

The borogoves grew thick and tall,
With vorpal thorns along each limb,
She gathered potions for them all,
Her mimsy bottles to the brim.

The frumious essences she'd blend,
With quogg-teeth ground and gribble-dust,
The wibble-petals she would send,
To those who came in frantic trust.

"The figlets dance!" the townfolk said,
"And see the crollops in her care!
She burbles spells upon our head,
And thrumbles circle everywhere!"

But she was kind, though tulgey-dressed,
Her snicker-snack of healing grace,
The manxome magic she possessed,
Brought comfort to each sickly face.

The glimmerwing would guard her door,
The beamish light she conjured shone,
The uffish remedies and more,
Had made her garden justly known.

Then outgrabe came the winter dark,
But mome and raths would still appear,
The fenland flowers left their mark,
And brought the frail ones through each year.

She never ceased her brillig work,
The slithy herbs forever grew,
Where potent powers ever lurk,
And frabjous cures forever brew.

'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
Did gyre and gimble in the wabe;
All mimsy were the borogoves,
And the mome raths outgrabe.

Beware the Whiffling, my beamish son!
The jaws that bite, the claws that snatch!
Beware the Glimmerwing, and shun
The frumious Burble-catch!

He took his vorpal blade in hand;
Long time the manxome foe he sought—
So rested by a Tulgey stand
Of sprack and vellumous thought.

And as in uffish thought he stood,
A Crollop, with eyes of flame,
Came whiffling through the fennish wood,
And burbled as it came!

Snicker-snack! He swung his blade!
One, two! One, two! And through and through
The vorpal gribble fell, afraid—
A snorfling scream rang true.

He fled in triumph through the night,
His beamish sword held high and bright;
The Glimmerwing took panicked flight,
All chortled at his might.

O frabjous day! Callooh! Callay!
He gallumphed back through morning's gleam;
The borogoves had run away,
And mome-raths nursed their dream.

'Twas brillig still, the day grew dim,
The wabe grew cold, the toves grew slow;
A figlet danced at fancy's brim,
Where lurgid shadows flow.

And now he waits by Tulgey wood
For Whifflings yet to come his way;
His vorpal blade stands sharp and good,
A hero's heart, both night and day.

'Twas morning, when the Blunder-sprites
Did crollop through the cloudish height;
The sky was thick with misty lights,
And wibbles danced in flight.

A slithy Quogg came spiraling down,
All mimsy-crowned with frost and rain;
It wore a burbled, silver gown,
And sang a sprack refrain.

Beware the Storm-Thrumbles, young one true!
They're galumphing across the air;
With vorpal gusts they'll come for you,
If you should not take care!

I ventured to the Tulgey moor,
Where fenish winds begin to blow;
And heard the Borogoves' outcry sore,
As thunder made its show.

The Glimmerwing came plored and slow,
With wings of vellumous delight;
It sang through all the wind and snow,
A beamish, chortled flight.

The Whiffling-clouds began to rage,
They burbled fierce and uffish-mad;
The sky became a stage
Where all the storm-sprites went quite bad.

I ran with feet of frumious speed,
Through scrim and figlet, dark and deep;
The Blunder-sprites, in manxome need,
Made thunder wake from sleep.

At last I reached the shelter-ground,
Where slithy toves did gyre and rest;
The Quogg came down without a sound,
And laid upon my chest.

The storm had passed, the dawn was clear,
The Glimmerwing flew west and far;
All borogoves lost all their fear,
Beneath the morning star.

In Tulgey depths where shadows plored,
A lurgid Figlet used to roam;
With wings of gribble, mimsy-stored,
It built its fenish home.

'Twas brillig when it started flight,
The wabe grew cold beneath its feet;
All slithy winds that howled all night
Would make the journey sweet.

Beware the Snibbet-creatures! Hark!
They're sprack and vellumous and sly;
They'll plore you in the dark,
And set your soul awry.

The Quogg came forth with burbled cry,
A manxome beast of storm and pain;
It gallumphed through the racing sky,
All chortled in the rain.

My vorpal blade I drew with haste,
While Borogoves began to flee;
The Glimmerwing came, uffish, braced,
To help defend with me.

We fought the Snibbet-swarm up high,
Where Whifflings danced in frumious bands;
The Blunder-sprites came screaming by,
With claws like grasping hands.

One, two! One, two! My blade went through!
The Figlet danced a victory reel;
The beamish sky came clear and blue,
And mome-raths ceased to squeal.

At last we rested in the wabe,
Where slithy toves did sing our praise;
The Crollop offered comfort grave,
And we beheld the coming days.

Come gather 'round, you curious folk,
And hear the tale of Thrumble-sprites;
In Tulgey wood, through fenish smoke,
They galumphed through the nights.

'Twas brillig, and the wind grew strong,
All mimsy clouds began to race;
The borogoves sang out their song,
While Whifflings roared through space.

A slithy Gribble, fierce and keen,
Came plored upon the morning air;
With vorpal wings of vellumous green,
It chortled everywhere.

Beware the Crollop's burbled call!
It draws the storm-sprites all around;
With manxome strength it conquers all,
And makes a uffish sound.

I took my blade, all sprack and bright,
And ventured to the Tulgey moor;
The Figlet danced throughout the fight,
While mome-raths fled the door.

The Blunder-sprites came one by one,
All lurgid-crowned with frozen rain;
But lo, my vorpal blade begun
To fill them all with pain.

The Glimmerwing came down to rest,
Upon my shoulder, soft and kind;
It knew that I had passed the test,
With scrim and figlet's mind.

At dawn I stood victorious, free,
The Quogg came forth to say farewell;
The beamish sky lay vast before me,
And all the borogoves did dwell.

Where Tulgey clouds do gyre and spin,
The Snibbet-storm came spiraling down;
All fenish winds came howling in,
And mimsy rain crowned every town.

'Twas brillig when the thunder woke,
The slithy toves began to flee;
Through wabe and burbled, swirling smoke,
Came Whifflings wild and free.

A vorpal Figlet danced on high,
With wings of vellumous, framing light;
It sang throughout the sprack-filled sky,
A beamish, uffish flight.

Beware the Crollop's manxome roar!
It shakes the very earth below;
The borogoves ran to the shore,
While Glimmerwings began to glow.

I stood and faced the storm-sprite host,
With blade in hand and courage strong;
Through scrim and figlet, coast to coast,
I chortled out my song.

The Quogg came burbled through the hail,
All gribble-crowned and lurgid-eyed;
Yet still I would not turn or fail,
With all the world my guide.

At last the tempest passed me by,
The mome-raths ventured out once more;
Beneath the clear and beamish sky,
We rested on the shore.

In morning's light of Tulgey-gold,
Where winds were sprack and shadows long,
A Glimmerwing, both brave and bold,
Did teach the clouds a song.

'Twas brillig when the Whiffling came,
All mimsy-crowned with dew and frost;
It chortled out its uffish name,
Through fenish paths, both lost.

Beware the Blunder-sprites that fly!
They're galumphing with frumious might;
They'll burble when they pass you by,
And plore you day and night.

A slithy Figlet, small and spry,
Came vellumous upon the breeze;
With vorpal heart it dared to try
To quiet all these frabjous pleas.

The Crollop wore a gribble crown,
All manxome-fierce and lurgid-wide;
It scrim-swept through the cloudy town,
With borogoves along its side.

I took my blade of snicker-snack,
And ventured through the wabe so deep;
The Quogg came wibbling at my back,
While mome-raths stirred from sleep.

One, two! One, two! The Snibbet fell!
The Whifflings scattered far away;
The beamish, sprack bells ceased to knell,
And peace returned to day.

The Tulgey wood grew calm and still,
Where once the storm-sprites danced and raged;
Beneath the bright and burbled hill,
Our victory was staged.

Where Tulgey depths grow dark and drear,
The Figlet came with wings of flame;
All mimsy creatures fled in fear,
When Glimmerwing began to claim.

'Twas brillig, and the slithy wabe
Grew thick with fog and fenish rain;
The borogoves began to crave
A beamish end to their refrain.

A vorpal Crollop, fierce and old,
Did gyre through all the sprack-filled air;
With manxome strength and heart so bold,
It filled the world with uffish care.

Beware the Whiffling's burbled cry!
It chortles when the thunder roars;
All gribble-crowned, it gallumphs by,
And plores the very core of yours.

I ventured to the storm-sprite's throne,
With blade in hand and courage true;
Through scrim and lurgid paths, alone,
The Quogg flew high, both fierce and blue.

The Snibbet-swarm came vellumous-fast,
All frumious and manxome-keen;
But mome-raths bound them to the past,
While Blunder-sprites could still be seen.

At last I faced the Tulgey beast,
That wibbled through the morning's glow;
One, two! The battle-fear had ceased,
And beamish victory could flow.

'Twas brillig in the morning's wake,
When Glimmerwings began their flight;
Through fenish clouds and mist they'd break,
All vellumous with silver light.

A slithy Whiffling, small and spry,
Did burble through the wabe so wide;
All mimsy borogoves drew nigh,
To walk along its side.

Beware the Figlet's sprack refrain!
It sings the storm-sprites all awake;
With uffish voice across the plain,
It makes the very thunder quake.

The Crollop came with gribble-crown,
All manxome-fierce and lurgid-slow;
Through scrim and fenish, up and down,
It made the cold winds blow.

A vorpal Quogg with burbled might,
Did chortled fight the Blunder-swarm;
The mome-raths danced throughout the night,
While Snibbet-sprites transformed.

I took my blade to join the fray,
Through Tulgey wood and wibble-dark;
The frumious beasts began to sway,
When fell my first great spark.

One, two! One, two! The battle raged,
Till plored and lurgid creatures fell;
The beamish dawn had been engaged,
And rang the frabjous bell.

At last we stood in morning's gold,
The Glimmerwing came to my side;
All mimsy borogoves, brave and bold,
Had conquered there with pride.

In Tulgey depths where shadows creep,
The Snibbet-creatures make their home;
All mimsy and so very deep,
Through fenish paths they roam.

'Twas brillig when I dared to go,
With vorpal blade held firm and true;
The wabe grew cold with uffish snow,
And Whifflings came into my view.

Beware the Figlet's frumious dance!
It burbles when the storm draws near;
With vellumous wings it takes its chance,
To fill the hearts of all with fear.

A slithy Crollop, old and wise,
Did gyre through all the scrim-filled air;
With manxome strength before my eyes,
It fought with borogove-like care.

The Glimmerwing came plored and slow,
All gribble-crowned with morning dew;
The Quogg with lurgid, beamish glow,
Did chortled what I knew to do.

The Blunder-sprites came sprack and bright,
All galumphing through the wabish rain;
But mome-raths danced throughout the fight,
And conquered all their pain.

One, two! One, two! My blade did slice!
The Snibbet-swarm began to fade;
With wibble-magic and with spice,
All frumious creatures were repaid.

At last the Tulgey wood grew calm,
Where once the tempest raged and roared;
Beneath the clear and beamish balm,
The peace we all adored.

Where fenish winds do howl and wail,
The Glimmerwing began to sing;
All mimsy creatures told the tale
Of storms that tempests bring.

'Twas brillig when the Figlet came,
With vorpal wings of silver-bright;
Through wabe and borogove's domain,
It gallumphed through the night.

Beware the Crollop's burbled call!
It chortles when the lightning strikes;
With manxome strength it conquers all,
And plores the things it likes.

A slithy Whiffling, uffish-crowned,
Did gyre through all the Tulgey moor;
With gribble-strength upon the ground,
It vellumous would roar.

The Quogg came scrim-swept from the sky,
All lurgid with its frumious might;
The Snibbet-swarm began to fly,
While mome-raths joined the fight.

I took my blade of snicker-snack,
And ventured through the wabish deep;
The Blunder-sprites came at my back,
While borogoves would weep.

One, two! One, two! The thunder fell!
All sprack and beamish creatures fled;
The wibble-magic broke the spell,
And light replaced the dread.

At dawn I stood with victory's grace,
The Glimmerwing came to my breast;
Beneath the clear and fenish space,
Our hearts had found their rest.

In depths of stone where glimmerwings do dwell,
A miner delved through galleries of night,
With vorpal pick he carved through cavern's shell
And sang to ease the weight of endless blight.

The tunnels bore such creatures rare and strange—
Stone-toves with eyes like quartz that caught the flame,
Their borogoves would shift along the range,
Each night returning always to the same.

He found one day a crystal thrumble there,
All vellumous and humming in the dark,
It spurned his hand and floated through the air,
Then vanished like a snorfling in the bark.

So still he digs where mountains crollop deep,
Where raths make mournful music in the ground,
And when the burden of the stone grows steep,
He rests and hears that glimmerwing's soft sound.

The wibbled crags above his head do waver,
Each footfall sends the gribbles running fast,
He tastes the lurgid dust of ancient savor—
The mountain's breath, the present and the past.

Yet down he goes where brillig never reaches,
Where shadows hold dominion over sight,
The stone itself becomes his faithful teacher:
That stone endures, while men must yield to night.

When comes the day his vorpal pick falls silent,
The thrumble will return and claim its own,
And all his labours, all his work resilient,
Will pass to feed the hunger of the stone.

So goes the miner, weary, unafraid,
Among the toves and creatures of the deep,
A man, a pick, a tunnel through the shade—
The mountain's vigil, endless and asleep.

In caverns far beneath the tulgey mountain,
There lived a gribble, ancient, wise, and strange,
Who guarded well a deep and silver fountain
That wibbled gently through its cavernous range.

The creatures came—the mimsy borogoves,
The slithy mome-raths digging all about,
The sprack-toves leaping over moonstone coves,
All seeking what the fountain was about.

"Come drink," the gribble burbled, "come and see
What waters flow from stone so deep below!"
But each who drank found they could never flee—
Their feet took root and they began to grow.

The borogoves became just stone themselves,
The toves turned hard as quartz, then turned to slate,
The gribble watched from deep within his shelves
Of crystal and of calcite—this their fate.

He was not cruel, this ancient one of stone,
But knew that some who seek the mountain's heart
Must stay within these halls of ancient bone
And never shall they ever once depart.

And still today, explorers wind the passages,
Where frozen toves hang gleaming on the wall,
And hear the old gribble send his messages:
"Turn back, turn back—the stone has claimed us all."

A cave-wyrm named Crollop did arise one spring,
All scales like slate and eyes of burnished ore,
He burbled hymns and made the caverns ring
With songs unheard in ten thousand years before.

The borogoves fled shrieking through the stone,
The thrumbles hid within their vellumous nests,
Poor Crollop sang, though singing was a groan—
He ached to leave, to fly beyond the crests.

He sculpted stairs of limestone with his tail,
He carved great doors from granite, floor to cave,
But every path and passage only failed,
The mountain held him like an endless grave.

One day there came a figlet through the door,
A creature small with glimmerwings so bright,
"Why do you weep, great wyrm?" the figlet swore,
"These caves are beautiful—they hold the light!"

And Crollop saw through this small creature's eyes
The jewels within the dark, the crystal clear,
The way the stone itself did crystallize
In patterns never rendered far from here.

He burbled softer then, a gentler song,
And found that he was not imprisoned quite—
That mountains held him, yes, but all along,
He'd been their voice, their voice throughout the night.

The lurgid motes of dust began to dance,
The gribbles crept to hear his melody,
And even Crollop's sorrow came to glance,
Upon the beauty of captivity.

In mining towns where borogoves once sprawled,
There came a peddler, curious and bent,
Who sold small stones, enchanted, carved and walled,
With promises of wonder in each spent.

"A glimmerwing?" said he, "I have it here—
Just place it on your shelf, it breathes the dark,
And when you doubt, when hope grows thin and sheer,
It glows within and leaves a gleaming mark."

The townspeople, both mome and man alike,
All bought his stones—they'd set them in their halls,
Each one would hum with some peculiar strike,
Each one would echo through their humbled walls.

But when the peddler finally left the town,
The stones grew still, their light began to fade,
And slowly, slowly, people wrote him down
As just a figment, just a clever trade.

Yet children still would find those stones and say,
"Look how it glimmers in the underground,"
And hum the tunes they'd heard the peddler play,
Before the mountain took him with no sound.

A party of explorers ventured down
Into a mine where no one'd gone before,
With vorpal picks and rope and map and crown
Of helmets bright—to find the ancient ore.

But deep below where passages turned twisted,
Where wibbled stone made corridors that spun,
The team grew small—at first two members misted,
Then three more vanished under mountain's sun.

The last man standing, quogg by name and trade,
Began to understand the mountain's way:
That those who delve within the cavern shade
Must leave some part of self along the way.

He found his friends transformed to glimmerwing,
No longer human, yet not wholly stone,
They hovered light as thought and did not sing,
But pulsed with knowledge never known.

"Come join us," whispered they, though without sound,
"We see the patterns written in the deep,"
But Quogg pressed on until he'd spun around
And clawed his way toward the world of sleep.

He burst from earth and gasped the open air,
His team still dancing far below the ground,
And tried to tell the world, "They're beautiful there!"—
But none believed a word of such a sound.

Upon a stone as broad as any field,
There sat a thrumble ancient, vellumous, wise,
Who'd learned from granite what the stone reveal'd,
And saw through calcite's many thousand eyes.

Each day the borogoves would come and ask,
"Great thrumble, how do mountains ever grow?"
And he would set them to a simple task:
"Go watch the water—stone's patient foe."

The toves came asking how to make their caves,
The gribbles sought the secret of their homes,
And still the thrumble gave to those who craves
A lesson written deep in mountain loams.

"The stone," he'd burble, "is not ever still,
Though you may think it rigid, blank, and dead,
It moves by will—not quick and sharp until,
But slow and steady as a dream is spread."

One visitor, a figlet young and keen,
Asked, "Thrumble, when the world is worn away,
What will remain of all we've ever seen?"
And thus the thrumble answered that same day:

"The mountains will remain when you are gone,
The caves will keep the memory you gave,
For stone remembers everyone that's known
And holds them gently in a crystal cave."

The figlet flew away with this in mind,
And told all creatures in the forest wide,
And those who sought such solace came to find
The thrumble sitting patient by its side.

In mines where lurgid fumes rose like a ghost,
There worked a crew of creatures brave and strange—
The slithy momes, the borogoves, a host
Of toves, all toiling through the vellum range.

They hammered, dug, and burbled ancient songs,
Their vorpal picks would snicker-snack the ore,
And though the work seemed endless, took so long,
Each creature loved the depths down to its core.

One day the earth began to gyre and shift,
The mountain trembled, quaked, began to moan,
A chasm opened—black, immense, and rift—
And swallowed down the caverns to the stone.

The miners fled, but one remained behind—
A borogove both mimsy, brave, and true,
Who stayed to guide the ones still blind and blind
To safety through the darkness breaking through.

She wibbled through the shaking stone and led
The toves and momes up through the twisted way,
Herself the last to leave that ancient bed,
To see the light again and break of day.

They built a monument of mined-up stone
In honor of her courage and her care,
And carved within so all would hear and own,
The story of the borogove so fair.

In winter deep, when brillig cannot reach
The caves and mines far underground below,
A creature made of stone will come and teach
A lesson older than the first of snow.

It moves so slow you'd scarce believe it moves,
This gribble born from calcite, slate, and lime,
It knows the paths that wind through ancient grooves,
And carries in its heart the sense of time.

The travelers who meet it never fear,
Though it speaks only in a grinding sound,
Yet somehow every word rings crystal clear:
"The stone remembers all you've ever found."

It leads them through the mountains, cool and deep,
Where thrumbles glow like stars beneath the ground,
And when the journey's weight grows dark and steep,
The creature's presence keeps them safe and sound.

By spring, the stone-thing slowly turns to go,
Back to the deep where creatures dwell of stone,
But those who've walked with it will ever know
That they are never truly quite alone.

For mountains hold their memory and care,
For those who've ventured deep within the shade,
And when you're lost in tunnels dark and bare,
Remember: stone is never one betrayed.

'Twas noon in the market at Snibble Fair,
When vendors with carts piled up to the sky
Did call for the folk both hither and there,
To taste of the Plimsauce and Thrumble-Pie.

The Quoggs in their aprons, all vellumous green,
Were stirring their pots with a vigorous whirr,
And children came running—the hungriest seen—
To snatch at the cakes dusted soft as a burr.

One Mome took a waffle, all figlet and sprack,
While Borogoves hummed in their bonnets of lace,
And crollops of candy were stacked in a stack,
Till half the bright market was worn on a face.

A Gribble sold sweets that were wibbling and warm,
And Toves that were slithy would gimble around,
While feasters and prancers danced into a swarm—
The finest fair feast in the whole of the ground.

'Til outgrabe the bell at the close of the day,
And vendors all packed up their curious goods,
And folk with their bellies went mimsy away,
To dream of Fair Snibble through sleep-tangled woods.

The Fenwick Estate held a feast, cold and lurgid,
Where Plored-beasts served soup in their platinum gowns,
And spoons made of Scrim-gold did glimmer and turgid,
While Glimmerwings fluttered above Plored-crowned towns.

No common pies sat upon any table here,
But Snorfling Delight in a tureen of mist,
And Burbled Mousse, which the learned held dear,
Made thick with the spittle of things that exist.

The Uffish Chief Butler stood beamish and tall,
With ladle of silver and gaze all askew,
And poured out a sauce that was Frumious tall,
That tasted of colours—vermillion and blue.

A Slithy guest giggled, all manxome and sly,
At the sight of the dessert that began to recite
Its own genealogy up to the sky,
And danced in the Whiffling flame-glow of night.

But soon came the Raths with their clattering spears,
And shattered the Fenwick Estate and its mood,
So revelers scattered like spilt chandeliers,
And lost was the feast midst the Tulgey wood.

The child on the doorstep sang into the rain,
A song about Plimsauce and Thrumbles and such,
How her grandmother's grandmother once entertained
A whole caravan's worth of the fabulous much.

She sang how the Borogoves baked with their wings,
And Toves made the Figlet so tender and light,
And Gribbles brought gifts in the shape of all things—
Bell-peppers and Burbles that glowed in the night.

Then mother came calling her indoors to sup,
On broth that was common, no creature at all,
But the child's voice still rang as she held up her cup—
"I'll dine with the Snorfling-folks one day, come fall."

In Crollop's dim kitchen, a lurgid and vast
Hall carved from the heartwood of Tulgey great trees,
An ancient receipt-book lay, creased by the past,
Was read by the cook with his whiffling-bound knees.

"A Plimsauce so fragrant," the recipe ran,
"Must bubble beneath with the breath of the Wabe,
Then cool in a Gimble—the old-fashioned plan—
'Til thick as a Mome's heart, and pale as a Scab."

The cook stirred and muttered and judged with his tongue,
While servants all tended the spit-roasted fowl,
And Figlets (in batter) were crisp-fried and strung
On ribbons of Scrim-silk, while Gribbles would howl.

But lo—came a knock—'twas no mortal at all,
A Vorpal-winged creature, all sprack-silver-bright,
Who'd smelled from the clouds this most fabulous hall,
And ventured on down through the Tulgey-dark night.

"I've journeyed through Wabe-fields," the creature did say,
"Through valleys of Gimble and forests of Blunder,
In hopes I might taste what I've dreamed every day—
A Plimsauce to make my whole being asunder."

So Crollop, all beamish, did bid him sit down,
And served him a portion, still smoking and bright,
And peace fell upon that peculiar town,
As Vorpal-beast feasted from dusk until night.

At dawn came the Toves in a snortling parade,
A hundred or more of them, slithy and wide,
Each carrying baskets of wares they had made—
Fresh Burbles and Figlets that bounced at each stride.

They set out their stalls in the Plored-stone plaza,
While Borogoves gossiped from awnings up high,
And Momes came awake with a stretching and "Hazah!"
To purchase the goods of the traveling supply.

The Gribbles sold candies all vellumous-sweet,
With flavorings drawn from the Tulgey-mist rare,
While customers queued with their purses in fleet,
To grab what they needed before daylight's glare.

One lad bought a Plimsauce, all figlet-en-lumped,
And bit through the skin where a shimmer did play,
And found that his tongue had completely been thumped
By tastes that had flavors of night turned to day.

But soon came a warning—the Uffish town crier—
Who rang out his bell with a mournful "Beware!"
For Raths had been sighted, all spitting and spire,
And Tulgey-beasts climbing the staircase of air.

The merchants all scattered, the Toves took to flight,
The Borogoves shrieked and their bonnets flew loose,
And people ran homeward with bags held up tight,
While Burbles and Figlets fell under the spruce.

The feast day had ended before it had truly begun,
But memory remains of that luminous brief
When Plored-stone and plenty and laughter and sun
Made Tulgey-town rich beyond measure—beyond belief.

In a shop made of Wabe-wood, all twisted and dark,
Sat Snibbet the cook (or so went the tale),
Who'd built up her fortune—her business, her mark—
By selling the rarest of edible scale.

Her Snorflings were famous a hundred towns wide,
Her Figlet-infusions worth walking for days,
Her Gimbles were perfect, her Plimsauce-fried
Left customers speaking her shop in a daze.

But Snibbet had never set foot on the street,
Never traveled beyond her small kitchen's warm glow,
But people brought stories with every treat—
Of markets and fairs and of all they did know.

One morning, a Vorpal-bird flew through her door,
All ruffled and weary from journeying far,
And dropped at her counter a letter with lore:
"Come see how I've loved you—beneath every star."

It bore the old scent of a Tulgey-wood grove,
And Snibbet, all Uffish, grew wibbled and strange,
For inside lay tales of a far-distant stove,
Where someone had cooked her recipes—made them range.

She locked up her kitchen, she followed the bird,
Through Wabe-fields and Blunder and Gimble-made streams,
To find in a castle the rarest she'd heard—
Her mother, alive in her deep-guarded dreams.

So feast-day came early that year, it is said,
In halls made of Figlet and Scrim-woven stone,
Where daughter and mother together then fed,
On Snorflings and Plimsauces finally come home.

'Twas in the month of mizzling gloom that I did set my pace,
Upon a road of quogg-stone laid through some forsaken place,
And there I met a figlet fair with wings of wibble-white,
Who burbled at me sweetly as she glimmered in the night.

"Good traveler," said she to me, "what brings you to these ways?
The bridges here are lurgid now, all tangled up with grays,
And those who venture outward find they seldom make return,
For all the paths are sprack with thorns that sting and twist and burn."

I told her that I'd journeyed far through many a tulgey wood,
Through fennish marshes, wibble-streams, wherever roads had stood,
And she, believing half my words, began to spin about,
Then disappeared like morning mist before I'd figured out.

I galumphed along the quogg-road still, with uffish gait and slow,
Past mome-hills where the borogoves were dancing in a row,
And when I reached a chasm deep with burbling sounds below,
I found a bridge of vellumous that seemed to softly glow.

I crossed it, though it thrumbled some beneath my weary feet,
And on the other side I found a village, quaint and sweet,
Where snarks were selling figlet-bread and snibbet-cakes to eat,
And all the folk were frabjous, dancing in the summer heat.

There lived an ancient crollop-sage who'd lived a thousand years,
And though his face was gribbled worn, he showed me not his fears,
He told me of a mountain pass that led to lands unknown,
Where crystal raths were singing songs in voices pure as stone.

I stayed there for a season long, and learned their ways so strange,
But wanderlust still burned within, a deep and restless change,
So when the spring began to thaw the snorfling in the air,
I packed my things and said goodbye to all the people there.

The crollop walked beside me to the edge where mountains rise,
And lifted up his gnarled hand to shield his ancient eyes,
"Come back when you have circled round the world beyond the blue,
Come back when you have found the place where slithy toves are true."

I climbed that pass through morning mist and days of whiffling snow,
Until at last I came upon a valley far below,
Where outgrabbing creatures dwelt in peace beneath the sun,
And there I built a dwelling where my travels were all done.

Yet sometimes in the brillig dusk I think about that road,
And all the quogg-stone paths I crossed, each strange and wondrous load,
The figlet wings, the burbling streams, the bridge of vellumous,
The crollop's final blessing—all these things I still discuss.

Through far-off lands and bridges strange I wandered, youth and age,
Through every sort of geography as if within a page,
And though I've settled finally where the raths still sing and call,
My heart still roams the quogg-roads—I'm not truly home at all.

Upon a morning mizzly-damp I woke beside a stream,
Where wibble-flowers nodded as if born inside a dream,
The road before me branched in three directions, none quite clear,
And standing at the junction was a snicker-snacking deer.

"Which way?" I asked the creature with his antlers all askew,
"Which way will lead to places I have never journeyed through?"
He pointed with his hoof toward where the tulgey shadows lay,
"But know that paths through darkness are not meant for folks to stray."

I thanked him for his counsel, though I heeded not his word,
For wandering is stronger than the wisest voice I've heard,
And so I took the darkest road through borogoves and grime,
Where figlets didn't flutter and the hours lost all time.

The ground grew soft beneath my feet, all squishy, thrumbling-dark,
Until I found a mansion made of sprack and gribbled bark,
Inside were rooms of vellumous, each one more strange than last,
Where snibbet-shadows danced about like ghosts of ages past.

An uffish thing with tentacles of lurgid, writhing grace,
Extended one appendage toward me, right across the space,
"You've come to find the answer to the question in your chest,
But first you'll join us here awhile, you'll be our honored guest."

They kept me there through burbling songs and meals of figlet-paste,
For years, I think, though time moved strange, all strangely displaced,
Until at last I broke away and galumphed through the door,
And found the road was waiting just exactly as before.

I stumbled back to brightness and a town of mome-folk kind,
Who fed me, gave me shelter, and helped settle my mind,
"That house," they said, "has taken souls for longer than we've known,
We thought that you were lost forever to that lurgid stone."

But I was not quite lost, you see, though changed forevermore,
For I had seen the ancient ways and crossed the hidden door,
And now I wander still among the roads and bridges made,
To help the lost and wandering come back before they fade.

A riddling voice called out to me from underneath a bridge,
"Answer this conundrum or you'll never cross this ridge:
What creature has the wings of quogg yet burbles like a stream,
And lives between the waking world and everyone's own dream?"

I thought upon this puzzle long, while figlets floated by,
And finally I answered with a somewhat weary sigh,
"It's memory," I told the voice, "it's what we carry on,
The way we hold the roads we've walked though many years have gone."

The voice began to chortled-laugh, a sound of mizzling glee,
"You've answered true, but here's a test—now answer this for me:
What bridge connects the places that we've never really been,
To everything we've only dreamed of or imagine in?"

I stood there with my thoughts all whirled like wibble-clouds above,
"It's hope," I finally whispered, "hope is what we speak thereof,
That bridge connects our present to some future yet unknown,
Where every road and every path will lead us safely home."

The riddling voice grew quiet then, I heard the waters flow,
And slowly from beneath the bridge a pathway came to show,
I walked across that bridge of hope with spirit light and free,
And found the roads diverged ahead in directions yet to be.

In lands beyond the outgrabbing where the raths still cry at night,
There lies a city made of stone beneath a vellumous light,
And all the travelers of the world eventually arrive,
To rest beside her fountains where the ancient roads survive.

I journeyed there through thrumbles dark and spracking winds of change,
Through every sort of landscape, wibbled, gribbled, strange,
And when I reached that city vast with spires in the air,
The figlets and the borogoves and mome-folk gathered there.

They'd come from every corner of the world both far and wide,
With stories of their journeys and the places they had spied,
And there we built a monument of lurgid, vellumous stone,
To mark the intersections where our separate roads had shown.

The monument displayed each path that every traveler knew,
The bridges that they'd crossed upon, the horizons they'd come through,
And carved upon its surface were the words both clear and true:
"All roads are one road, winding through—all journeys lead us through."

I stayed there for a goodly time and shared my tales as well,
Of quogg-stone paths and figlet-wings and bridges I could tell,
Of uffish creatures, thrumbling sounds, and cities made of dreams,
Of all the wondrous places found beside the burbling streams.

But restlessness, that ancient friend, grew strong within once more,
So I set out from that great city, leaving shore for shore,
The roads stretched out before me in directions endlessly,
And somewhere there beyond the mist, new roads await for me.

The wind came down from mountain heights with snorfling, chilling song,
I'd walked the roads through many years, though not quite clear how long,
When suddenly I stumbled on an archway made of sprack,
And when I passed beyond its frame, I couldn't find way back.

The landscape shifted all around, the colors grew most strange,
The roads beneath my feet began to quiver, twist, and change,
I saw a quogg-stone pathway lead toward a distant spire,
And heard a voice of figlets singing songs around a fire.

I followed toward that calling sound through wibble-trees and vines,
Till I arrived at crossroads marked with ancient, rune-like signs,
A snicker-snacking sphinx was there, both terrible and kind,
"The roads," she said, "that brought you here will never you remind—

Of who you were before you walked these paths forevermore,
You've journeyed to the center now, you've reached the hidden core,
Where every road does truly lead, where all the bridges meet,
Where travelers become the road, and walking makes complete."

I felt myself transforming then, my body turning stone,
My consciousness extending down through every road I'd known,
And in that moment of becoming, I could see it clear and true—
That I myself was every path that ever journeys through.

I felt the weight of countless feet from ages long forgotten,
I felt the dreams of wanderers both blessed and most downtrodden,
I felt the hope and weariness of every soul who'd strayed,
From every realm of brillig-time to every far-off glade.

And now I am the road itself, the bridge that carries all,
The path that leads to mystery, both majestic and so small,
And every traveler who comes will walk upon my back,
And find within the journey done, whatever they did lack.

'Twas in the spring when greening thaws had broken
The frozen wabe where mimsy toves did sleep,
And borogoves, though hardly yet bespoken,
Began to stir from winter's vigil deep.
A young mome crept through gribble'd paths and hollow,
His fur still thin, his eyes not yet quite keen,
And all the flowers that came did seem to follow
His fumbling steps through sprack and verdant sheen.
"Come hither, child," the eldest borogove cried,
"The season calls—you must learn raths to seek,
To gyre and gimble with a slithy glide,
And know which burbled streams run fresh and meek."
But still the mome went whiffling through the morning,
Half-sleepy still, and slow to understand
That spring was not a game without a warning—
That growing meant a claim upon the land.
When brillig came, the toves began their snapping,
And all the young momes trembled at the sound,
Yet he had learned by then, through spring's long lapping,
That change was root and reason, deep and bound.

By summer's height the youngmome, now sprack-footed,
Could leap through tulgey thickets without fear,
Where glimmerwings in multitudes uprooted
The quiet darkness that had ruled the year.
He'd met a figlet, frumious and kind,
Who taught him how to navigate the maze
Of borogove-song and vorpal-bordered rind,
And how to read the wibble-written ways.
Together they would galumph through the meadow,
Where quoggs emerged from fennish, churning ground,
And cast their long and ever-lengthening shadow
Across the thrumbles that grew all around.
"Next winter comes," the figlet said one evening,
"When all of us must shed what we have grown,
And you will find your earlier, brief believing
Has ripened into knowing, hard and known."
The youngmome listened, burbling soft and low,
And felt the warmth of friendship ease his dread—
That growing older needn't only show
A loss of wonder, innocence, instead.

In autumn's month when leaves grew lurgid, golden,
The mome began to sense a subtle call,
A pull toward the paths of those grown old when
The great wheel turned, preparing for the fall.
He'd learned to outgrabe with a proper snicker-snack,
And earned his place among the slithy crews,
Yet something nagged—a longing to turn back
To spring's small clearing and the morning dews.
A crollop-bird, those creatures half-between things,
Alighted on a branch above his head:
"You mourn," it said, "for what the seasons bring—
The fading light, the golden turning red."
"But hark," it burbled, "mark what I unfold:
Each year you'll find new wonders yet to seize,
And what you lose in youth, you'll gain in gold—
The strength to stand alone among the trees."
The autumn wind came down with one last warning,
And all the toves grew still and thummoxed, strange,
But when the mome woke up that final morning,
He faced the coming winter without change.

The plored expanse of snibbet-laden winter
Found our young mome now toughened by the year,
With knowledge earned through every season's glimmer,
A steadier and more magnificent career.
He built a burrow deep where none could find him,
Yet not in fear—in dignity and pride,
For he had learned what time would soon remind him:
That growing strong means learning when to hide.
The quoggs passed by in gangs of wibble-sniffing,
The borogoves sang songs of ages past,
And still the young mome, never once shrift-iffing,
Kept faith that spring would come around at last.
A memory of that first time, green and tender,
When he had barely known his own small name,
Burned bright within like some eternal ember—
The root from which he'd grown into this frame.
And deep beneath the snow and thrumble-tangle,
He slept and dreamed of seasons yet to come,
No longer lost within his own strange wrangle,
But centered, whole, and finally found home.

In that far land where seasons dance togither,
There lived a quogg of most peculiar skill,
Who'd learned to switch his coat with every slither,
From spring's bright green to winter's silver chill.
But he grew weary of the constant changing,
And asked the ancient tove of all the wood:
"Why must I shed and gyre, forever arranging
My different selves? Can't one form be good?"
The tove, all slithy-wise and old and frumious,
Did burble out a truth both fierce and true:
"The quogg who seeks to stand forever uniform
Will find himself has lost what makes him new.
For in the ebb and flow of all the seasons,
You gather gifts you never could possess
If you remained immobile—reasons
Upon reasons ripen through the stress."
And so the quogg embraced his ever-shifting
Dance through the wabe with snicker-snacking grace,
Found joy in each new form and in the drifting
Of one more version of his borrowed face.
The moral, dear ones, if you should be seeking,
Is this: though change is hard and sometimes deep,
'Tis in the turning that we're really speaking
Of what it means to grow, and grow, and keep.

A lullaby for all the little borogoves
Who fear the passing of their cherished spring:
The wabe grows soft with time, not harsh but cloves,
And every season brings some precious thing.
Hush now, don't cry because the blooms must wither,
The world is full of changes yet untold,
Each moment that you leave behind you'll glitter
In memory, more beautiful and bold.
Sleep soundly in the tulgey wood tonight,
While all the glimmerwings dance through the dark,
Tomorrow brings a new and different light,
A fresher way to follow, brighter spark.
The toves will gather round you as you're sleeping,
And whisper how they, too, once used to fear
That when one season faded in its keeping,
They'd lose forever what they held so dear.
But no—the spring returns, though not the same,
With different flowers, different warming sun,
Yet still it kindles that familiar flame,
That tells us life continues, never done.

There once was a mome who could never decide
Whether to grow big or to stay small,
So he'd wibble and wobble from side to side,
And never appeared to age at all.
The seasons came round with their usual rhyme,
The toves would galumph and the quoggs would shout,
But this indecisive mome marked time
By always deferring, waffling out.
"Choose now!" cried a snorfling with vorpal jaws,
"For dithering between two states is death—
You'll lose the vigor that the growing draws,
And find yourself with none of your own breath."
The mome, at last, took courage in his trembling,
And chose to climb toward his fullest height,
Though still within him stirred a soft dissembling—
The love of littleness, small and tight.
Yet here's the gift that growing finally granted:
He found that he could hold both truths at once,
That being larger didn't mean supplanted
The sense of wonder, innocence, and puns.
He grew and kept his childhood close beside him,
Not buried deep or cast away in shame,
And in that marriage of the old and rid'em,
He found at last a most peculiar fame.

A riddle wrapped within the autumn gloaming:
What walks on three legs in the fading year,
Yet in the spring returns to two-leg roaming,
And speaks in burbles only toves can hear?
The answer lies in neither beast nor creature,
But in the way that time has come to bend—
For every living thing must own the feature
Of knowing where to start and where to end.
A glimmerwing once asked this very question
Of all the wisdom-keepers in the wood,
And each one gave a different aged suggestion,
Though each was true and rightly understood.
The eldest borogove, with voice most solemn,
Said: "Time is not a straight and narrow track,
But rather like the chapters of a column—
Each closes out, yet nothing takes it back."
And so the young mome grasped the deeper meaning:
That seasons turn not to erase the past,
But rather like a cloth, with every leaning,
Creating something richer, dense, and vast.
From spring through winter, summer through the plored expanse,
Each mome learns at last to understand that dance.

In that deep place where mimsy toves grow restless,
There dwelt a figlet, cunning and afraid,
Who'd heard that time would make all things defenseless,
And so she hid herself within the shade.
She watched the other creatures bloom and flourish,
Saw momes grow strong and quoggs grow bold and bright,
Yet still she clung to safety, tried to nourish
Her fear by staying hidden out of sight.
But winter came with all its thrumbles crashing,
And buried deep the warren where she'd stayed,
And she was forced to venture, through and bashing
Through snow and ice and every obstacle made.
By spring she'd earned a strength she never knew,
And found that facing fear had set her free—
She'd grown not just in body and sinew,
But in her spirit, boundless and at sea.
The other creatures, seeing her transformed,
Came close and asked for stories of her tale,
And she, no longer timid, newly formed,
Spoke truth in burbles that would never pale.
She learned that sometimes growing means to venture,
Past all the walls we've built to keep us safe,
And that the courage to step beyond the entry
Is what allows us all to truly chafe.

Upon a wibble-woven path, one morning,
There came a most unusual kind of train
Of creatures—momes and toves, without a warning,
All heading toward some distant, misty plain.
A young mome asked, "Where does this journey lead us?"
And one old tove with eyes like golden gleams
Said, "Onward, always onward—that's the creed, thus
We follow where the seasons call our dreams."
They walked through spring and summer, burbling softly,
Past all the landmarks, gribbles, fernish grounds,
While each one shed their past lives slowly, often,
Yet gathered new companions all around.
The journey was not easy—some fell weary,
And some turned back to places they had known,
But those who pressed ahead, though dark and dreary,
Found they had made a strength that was their own.
By autumn, when they reached that distant nation,
Each creature bore a glow of hard-earned grace,
No longer bound by youthful limitation,
But carrying new wisdom in their face.
The moral written plain for all to read it:
The greatest gift of growing is the road—
Each step you take, each challenge that you heed it,
Becomes the strength you carry as your load.

'Twas late within a tickle-hall so grimly grim,
Where clockwise gears did turn and churn so very dim,
When in there came a sprock-like beast, a fumbled thing,
With sprocket-toes that clicked and clocked and made bells ring.

It wound about the copper tubes with snibbet-grace,
And left behind a glimmerwing of oily trace,
The cogs did spin in manic glee, thrumble-thrumble-THRUM,
As oil-drops fell like dewdrops bright—dum-dum-dum-dum!

Then in there crept a crollop-mouse, so small and sly,
To steal the springs and steal away beneath the sky,
But caught it was! The beast did whiff and whiffle round,
And chased the wee thing through each shaft with gribble-sound.

They galumphed past the pendulums that swung so true,
And climbed upon the lurgid weights of leaden blue,
Till finally the crollop-mouse did leap and bound,
And vanished in the vellumous old clockwork ground.

The sprock-beast stood and stood there, uffish quite and still,
Its sprocket-toes lay idle on the metal sill,
For time, you see, had stopped its tick, had ceased to know,
And all the gears lay silent in their glow below.

So now they say when midnight chimes in that old place,
You'll hear a click, a whiffle-laugh, a ghostly trace,
Of how a beast and mouse once danced the spring-time waltz,
And broke forever all the clockwork's measured halts.

The tickle-hall stands empty now, no soul dares near,
For fear the gears might start again throughout the year,
And from those depths, with snicker-snack so sharp and keen,
Might come those things that ought not be, but once have been.

A shop there was in tulgey times, where toys grew strange,
Where in a corner sat a thing of twisted range—
A figlet-doll with button-eyes of burnished brass,
That wound itself and walked about upon the glass.

The shopkeep wound it every dawn with shaking hand,
Yet every dusk it moved itself, as if it'd planned,
He watched it spin and pirouette with sprackish grace,
And saw the faintest smile upon its wooden face.

One night he followed where it went with crollop-creep,
Through winding lanes of fennish dark and ditches deep,
Until they reached a glade where other toys stood round,
All dancing to a music that made not a sound.

The figlet-doll turned slowly round and looked at him,
Its brazen eyes grew ever bright, its outline dim,
And in that gaze he understood what he had made—
Not toy, but friend, and friend now chose to walk, unswayed.

So home he went and left the key upon the shelf,
And every night the figlet-doll became itself,
And now the townsfolk swear they've seen that doll parade,
With all its toy companions through the tulgey glade.

They say at last the shopkeep died content and old,
For he had built a thing that could itself be bold,
A toy that needed not a hand to make it move,
But danced instead from something born of love to prove.

Three brothers made a contraption vast and grand,
With levers, wheels, and whiffling gears worked hand in hand,
They said, "This thing shall plore the deepest darkest scrim,
And tell us what lies hidden past reality's rim."

They pressed the button made of burnished silver-stone,
And heard a sound they'd never made nor ever known,
A grinding, churning, thrumble-thrumble symphony,
As gears did spin towards infinity, infinity!

The machine grew hot, the lights grew bright, the walls did shake,
And in that moment, for their trembling bodies' sake,
They saw right through the fabric of the waking world,
To where the secret borogoves had long been curled.

But then—alas!—the contraption's end did come to pass,
It shattered into glimmerwings and shattered glass,
And all three brothers tumbled back to normal sight,
With memories of visions burning cold and white.

They tried to build it once again with greater care,
But something in the pattern floated through the air,
Escaped, you see, when first they glimped beyond the veil—
A creature born of understanding, born of tale.

Now through the tulgey forests comes a thing of light,
With gribble-feet and snicker-snack teeth gleaming white,
And townspeople say brotherly it came to roam,
Born from the brothers' wonder, now it seeks a home.

In nurseries where children sleep in deep repose,
There sits a toy that nobody but baby knows,
A burbled thing of quilted cloth and beamish charm,
That keeps the nightmares distant, keeps the child from harm.

At three o'clock when darkness presses down most tight,
The toy comes gently shimmering with silver light,
And rocks the cradle gently with its mome-like paws,
While humming lullabies of old, without a pause.

The mothers find the nurseries are calm and cold,
Yet warm as if ten thousand stories have been told,
The babies grow up smiley, kind, and full of grace,
With dimples deep as borogove-holes in that place.

But none recall the guardian who kept them safe,
The toy dissolves like morning mist, like morning chafe,
And mothers find a empty cot, a glimmerwing thread,
A memory of something that was never said.

In ancient shops the servants found the toys all gone,
Replaced by empty boxes at the break of dawn,
And swear that they had never seen that quilted thing,
Yet every child born there grows up with joy to sing.

A clockmaker of old did build a most queer sight—
A music-box of vellumous and lurgid light,
That played a tune in backwards time, in reverse-way,
Where every note came last before it came to play.

The townsfolk gathered round to hear this strange contraption work,
And listened to the melody that hid itself in murk,
For every note hung silent til the song had passed,
Then spoke itself out loud—the first note came in last!

A little girl sat captive by the sound's strange spell,
And danced to rhythms that the future soon would tell,
She spun and pirouetted to a song unborn,
Predancing all her steps before that gift morn.

The clockmaker grew worried as he watched her move,
For she was dancing motions that she'd need to prove,
And when the music ended at the backward start,
She'd lived her life already, bless her gifted heart.

He tried to stop the music-box and break its spring,
But found the girl had faded like a snicker-snack thing,
She lives now in that backwards song, forever free,
Still dancing all her futures for eternity.

There was a riddle carved upon a wooden box,
With spring-wound wheels and figlet-locks and ticking clocks,
"Solve me," said the box unto a weary uffish soul,
"And open shall my secrets from my burnished hole."

The traveler sat down upon the wabbled ground,
And pondered long the riddle's twists and woven sound:
"I tick but have no heart, I move but have no feet,
I wind up time itself—now make this answer neat!"

He thought and thought till morning came with silver rays,
And suddenly he understood through clouded haze:
"You are the thing that measures out the days we've spent,
The keeper of our moments, the constraint, the bent!"

But when he spoke the answer clear and true and straight,
The box did not spring open up its puzzle-gate,
Instead it whispered softly from its copper breast,
"You've found the question, friend, but not the one I've blessed."

For every clock and every watch and every bell,
Contains within its mechanism one last spell—
