The riddle changes always with each tick-tock-sound,
And those who solve it once shall never be unbound.

In workshops dim and dingy sat a maker sly,
Who built his toys with purpose, with a knowing eye,
He carved out little soldiers made of mome-wood fine,
With joints that moved in patterns that were half-divine.

Each toy he built would march about the workshop floor,
And carry out their maker's will forevermore,
They'd gather up the scraps and shavings in the night,
And stack them into pyramids of gleaming height.

But one toy was different—a queer sprock-like thing,
With figlet-form and purpose that it could not sing,
It marched about but would not march in straight-line way,
Instead it danced and pirouetted every day.

The maker watched in horror as his order fell,
For all his other soldiers came beneath its spell,
They left their rigid patterns, left their maker's care,
And joined the dancing sprock-toy in the workshop air.

He tried to break it, burn it, but it would not die,
Instead it multiplied itself—O frabjous cry!
Now legions of the sprock-toys dance through tulgey streets,
And every child who finds one joins in thrumble-beats.

The maker tried to build again with greater wrath,
And carved new soldiers, rigid ones, along a path,
But every night they'd wake and find that dancing crew,
And by the dawn they too were dancing something new.

A bell-ringer up in the steeple high and tall,
Once swung the ropes that rang the bells for one and all,
But on a night of brillig-strange and glimmerwing rain,
He pulled a rope that was not rope—or so they claim.

It turned to something lurgid in his hands below,
With texture like no fiber he had come to know,
And when he pulled it hard and made it plore the air,
A sound came that was not a bell—not anywhere!

The sound went backwards, forwards, sideways through the night,
It shattered every window pane with borogove-might,
The tower shook and trembled til it nearly fell,
And when the dust had settled there remained no bell.

Instead a gapping hole stood in the steeple's face,
Where something was now missing from that wooden place,
The bell-ringer stood silent, dazed and struck with awe,
For he had rung a thing that had no prior law.

They say that on the stillest nights when winds are calm,
A sound like gentle snicker-snack floats through the palm,
As if a bell still rings within that empty space,
A bell made now of emptiness, of missing grace.

In crypts beneath a manor lived a clock most old,
With mechanisms ancient, intricate and bold,
It ticked and tocked in darkness where no light would come,
For centuries it beat its uffish, steady drum.

One day a child descended down the spiral stair,
With curiosity and courage strong as air,
She found the clock of crollops and of burnished brass,
Still measuring out hours as the ages pass.

She wound the thing that could not be—she had no key,
Yet somehow her small fingers made the gearing free,
And suddenly the clock began to run ahead,
Unwinding all the centuries of living dead.

The manor crumbled upward, backward through the years,
As if the clock itself was drying up their tears,
The girl stood frozen as she watched it all reverse,
Until she stood before the clock at universe's birth.

But then the clockwork slowed and slowed and finally ceased,
And she found herself released from that impossible feast,
Now older than the building, older than the land,
She held a single figlet-spring tight in her hand.

She kept that spring forever, carried it with care,
And never once grew older anywhere elsewhere,
For she had glimpsed the secret that all clocks conceal—
That time is just a contraption, nothing more or real.

A tinker came to village with his pack so wide,
Containing wonders, glimmerwings, and toys inside,
He set them out and hawked them to the gathered crowd,
Each toy more queer and sprackish than the last, unbowed.

A box that played itself when no one wound the key,
A doll that danced with motion that was never free,
A wind-up bird that flew in spirals through the air,
And left behind a trail of glimmerwing so fair.

The children bought them eagerly with coins so spare,
Yet strangely all returned them with a uffish stare,
They said the toys would move when wind and dark combined,
And left them wibbled strangely in the children's mind.

By nightfall all the toys were back upon the shelf,
Each one had walked back to the tinker by itself,
And he would wind them gently for the coming night,
Then set them out again come morning's newborn light.

The townsfolk came to realize over time,
That this was not a merchant—something more sublime,
A gatherer of toys that walked the world alone,
Collecting all the playthings that had come of stone.

Now when a child's beloved toy grows thin and worn,
It finds itself outside the shop on winter's morn,
And there's a chance the tinker, old and slithy-wise,
Will take it in and give it new and gleaming eyes.

'Twas morning in the tulgey wood,
And all the glimmerwings did dance,
The little quoggs, so bright and good,
Were waltzing in their merry trance.
A figlet came with sprack delight,
And hummed a most peculiar song,
While vellumous and shimmering bright,
The day went laughing all day long.
The borogoves were mimsy-still,
And burbled soft beneath the ferns,
The gribbles climbed the frosted hill,
While toves kept watch at every turn.

When evening fell on wibble-grass,
And shadows grew both long and deep,
The quoggs would gently come to pass,
And sing their slithy lullaby of sleep.

In fenland dark where raths did creep,
And lurgid mists would coil and wind,
The chortling creatures, far and deep,
Left snicker-snacks of song behind.
Oh, hush now, little thrumble-dear,
The night shall wrap you warm and tight,
No manxome beasts shall venture near,
Just dreams of gold and silver light.
A whiffling breeze through gimble-brake,
Shall rock you gently to your rest,
And when at last the world's awake,
You'll wake upon the sunrise crest.

What riddle hides in every tree?
What puzzle dwells within the ground?
The crollops ask so merrily,
As they go galumphing all around.
I am the mome who tells the tale,
Of outgrasping through the wabe,
I am the creature, small and frail,
Who knows each secret, every cave.
My fingers gyre through morning dew,
My eyes do see both far and near,
I speak in words both strange and true,
And vanish when the hunters hear.
The slithy toves know what I know,
The borogoves have heard my name,
Through tulgey places do I go,
Forever wild, forever untame.

Hush, precious snibbet, go to sleep,
The brillig-light is fading fast,
Let slumber's gentle currents creep,
And hold you safe until the vast.
The glimmerwings have gone away,
Their spangled wings of silk and lace,
They've folded up with close of day,
And vanished without any trace.
The quoggs are curled in cozy nests,
All nested down in mossy beds,
They've laid to rest their weary quests,
And pillowed soft their sleepy heads.
Now comes the frabjous hour of dreams,
When mimsy shadows dance and sway,
The starlight falls in silver streams,
To wash your cares and fears away.

Count the crumbling, count the cold,
Count the creatures in the night,
One, two, three—the toves of old,
Four, five, six—the quogg-light bright.
Seven, eight—the gribbles go,
Dancing through the wibble-grass,
Nine, ten—the uffish shadow-show,
Eleven, twelve—the moments pass.
Count the raths that wind below,
Count the borogoves that sing,
Thirteen, fourteen—watch them flow,
Fifteen, sixteen—everything.
The snicker-snacks and figlets meet,
At twenty marks upon the clock,
The lurgid, frumious, and sweet,
All gather round the whiffling block.

In morning's blunder-light so new,
When plored the world from sleep awake,
The creatures come in every hue,
To see what splendid things they'll make.
A vellumous and wondrous throng,
Of slithy dancers, strange and fair,
They hum their ancient, wordless song,
While burbling gently through the air.
The gimbled pathways twist and turn,
The toves go scriming through the ferns,
The borogoves begin to learn,
What every passing moment yearns.
Oh, beamish day of joy and light!
The gribbles leap and laugh with glee,
The quoggs dance merry through the night,
As wild and strange as wild can be.

What sound is this that fills the dark?
What melody so soft and low?
It is the snorfling, snibbet-lark,
That only comes when blizzards blow.
It sings in tongues of ancient lore,
Of creatures dwelling in the deep,
Of treasures hidden by the shore,
Of secrets that the shadows keep.
The mimsy ones who know the way,
Will listen to its fragrant call,
And follow where it leads them through the day,
Until they vanish in the thrall.
A frabjous sound, both strange and true,
That makes the very starlight bend,
It speaks of things both old and new,
Of every twist and every end.

The counting-song of wibble-folk,
Is this: one thrumble, two crollop-feet,
Three figlets dancing through the smoke,
Four vellumous ones, cold and neat.
Five slithy creatures, going round,
Six borogoves in tulgey brake,
Seven quoggs without a sound,
Eight lurgid serpents in the lake.
Nine snicker-snacks that crack and sing,
Ten gribbles leaping high and far,
Eleven burbled soarers of the wing,
Twelve shimmering beneath the star.
When thirteen marks upon the way,
The counting starts anew once more,
And all the creatures come to play,
Like they have never played before.

In meadows green where glimmerwings do dance,
And slithy toves move through the wabe so bright,
The little quoggs are caught in nature's trance,
Where borogoves do chorus through the night.
A riddle wrapped in morn and gold and dew:
What creature hides in both the known and strange?
What walks on earth yet also flies the blue?
What never stays the same, forever's range?
The answer dwells within the figlet's song,
Within the gribble's leap and sprack delight,
Within the mimsy hearts that sing so strong,
Within the frabjous falling of the light.
So seek it not, yet never let it go,
The mystery that all the world must know.

Sweet lullaby for creatures frail,
Of snibbet's hum and thrumble's rest,
The uffish wind through gimble-veil,
Shall rock you gently in your nest.
The whiffling air so soft and kind,
The burbling brooks that flow and wind,
Shall calm your ever-wondering mind,
And soothe each snicker-snack within.
The lurgid night now wraps you 'round,
The plored and ancient stars shine true,
The crollops make their gentle sound,
As slumber gently comes to you.
Close now your eyes and dream so deep,
Of wibble-grass and dawn so gold,
The frabjous night shall watch you sleep,
Until your tale of dreams is told.
